title: What Our Backtest Says About the Senate Model
dek: Our calibration page shows a model that is still being tested, but not one that is failing. The archived-input backtest is the main calibration source, while the live diagnostic is a temporary stress test that will be cleaned up by May 23, 2026.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: A forecast model should not be judged only by whether it picks winners. It should also be judged by calibration. If a model gives candidates a 65 percent chance to win, candidates in that range should win close to 65 percent of the time across enough races.

Our Senate model is still early in its calibration work. The page currently shows two different tests, and that has caused some confusion. The archived-input backtest is the main one to use. The current diagnostic is more of a live-model stress test.

The archived-input backtest is the cleaner test because it uses frozen historical inputs. That means it asks a direct question. If this model had existed with past-cycle information, how close would it have been?

The answer so far is positive, but incomplete. The archived-input sample currently has 11 races. That is not enough for a final verdict, but it is enough to see whether the model is behaving in a reasonable way.

In the archived-input test, the 50 to 60 percent bucket went 2 for 2. The 60 to 70 percent bucket went 3 for 4. The 70 to 80 percent bucket went 2 for 2. The 80 to 90 percent bucket went 3 for 3. The 90 to 100 percent bucket has no races yet.

Those results defend the model better than a simple win-loss record would. The model is not missing races in a random or chaotic way. The early archived-input test suggests the model is sorting races into reasonable probability ranges.

The main limit is sample size. A bucket with two or three races does not prove perfect calibration. It only tells us the model has started in the right direction. More archived cycles are needed before the calibration score should be treated as stable.

The current diagnostic has a larger 35-race sample, but it is not the full calibration test. It compares the live model shape against each state's latest available Senate result. That helps find risk areas, but it is not the same as using frozen historical forecast inputs.

That distinction matters. The current diagnostic includes states where the comparison is not a clean election-to-election match. Some states use 2016 or 2018 comparisons. Some have little polling. Some have major candidate differences. Some have current-cycle conditions that differ from the last Senate race.

That is why the current diagnostic should not be used as the main grade for the model. It is useful as a warning system. It shows where the model might be too confident, too cautious, or too dependent on state fundamentals. It does not replace the archived-input test.

Even with those limits, the current diagnostic does not show a broken model. The 60 to 70 percent bucket has a 62.5 percent historical win rate against a 65 percent expected win rate. The 90 to 100 percent bucket has a 95 percent historical win rate against a 95 percent expected win rate. Those are strong signs.

The weakest-looking area is the 80 to 90 percent bucket, where the current diagnostic shows a 33.3 percent historical win rate from only three races. That should be watched, but not overread. Three races are not enough to prove the model is overconfident in that range.

The archived-input misses are also not alarming. The largest archived-input misses are Pennsylvania at 5.2 points, Wisconsin at 4.2 points, Ohio at 3.6 points, Nebraska at 3.4 points, Nevada at 3.3 points, Florida at 2.8 points, Arizona at 2.6 points, and Montana at 2.1 points.

Those misses are normal for Senate forecasting. Senate races are candidate-driven. State polling is often sparse. Independent campaigns, open seats, incumbency effects, and late-cycle shifts all create uncertainty. A model that misses several races by two to five points is not failing. It is operating within a normal error range.

The model's mean Brier score in the current diagnostic is 0.143, and the mean margin miss is 12.5 points. That margin number looks high, but it comes from a diagnostic that includes imperfect comparisons. The largest margin misses panel even flags several cases where the historical comparison does not match a frozen 2026-like pre-election snapshot.

That is the main source of confusion on the page. One section is a cleaner archived-input backtest. The other section is a live diagnostic that compares current model behavior against past results. Both are useful, but they should not be read the same way.

By May 23, 2026, we plan to finish the calibration cleanup and end this confusion. The goal is to make the page clearer, separate archived-input calibration from live diagnostics, and expand the historical backtest so readers know which numbers matter most.

The model should be defended honestly. It is not fully validated yet. It does not have enough archived races yet. Some buckets are still too small. Some diagnostic comparisons are noisy. But the available evidence does not show a bad model.

The better read is this. The archived-input backtest is promising. The live diagnostic is useful but imperfect. The model has normal Senate-forecasting error, not evidence of collapse. More archived cycles will make the calibration page stronger.

For now, the archived-input backtest should be treated as the main calibration source. The current diagnostic should be treated as a stress test. Once the May 23 cleanup is complete, the model will have a clearer calibration system and a more direct way to judge its accuracy.

title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered in any pathway to victory for Democrats in 2026 when it comes to the Senate. This is in large part because Republicans dominate the state. Democrats struggle in deep-red Nebraska due to negative brand recognition. AP reported that Nebraska Democrats in 2026 are looking for others who can "outperform the Democratic label."

Osborn is in a different form. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He campaigns on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close historically in Nebraska. Fischer won by only about six points, while in 2024, the state voted for Donald Trump by over 20 points. What we learned was simple. Some voters who might reject national Democrats would still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

Just last week, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned simply on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. This reduces a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race, which all but guarantees Republicans hold on in the state.

Nebraska Democrats appeared to understand that when Nebraska's race focuses on the national aspect, Ricketts wins. When it goes local, Osborn stands to benefit. This is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic.

Of course, this does not work anywhere. You need someone with local credibility and a message voters believe. In a state where voters have histories of ticket splitting or independents, it might be the right move. However, national Democrats must stay disciplined. If these independents are turned into Republican versus not Republican, the brand is weakened.

Even if what the forecast model says holds, and Osborn loses, the current projected margin of only 3.9 points Republican shares a big message. Democrats must reinvent their strategies in the deep red, or become a figment of the past for those living in red states.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.
